source.title: Ask Me Anything: A simple strategy for prompting language models
source.authors: Simran Arora; A. Narayan; Mayee F. Chen; Laurel J. Orr; Neel Guha; Kush Bhatia; Ines Chami; Frederic Sala; Christopher Ré

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites scaling-law work and discusses model size, but it does not test held-out pretraining loss scaling, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or the other listed versions. Its own scale-related results concern the effect of the AMA prompting method, not the claimed scaling laws.
record.gate_note: No result measures held-out cross-entropy loss, fits or extrapolates a loss power law, tests compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or compares architecture shape or other modalities. The paper's model-size and conditional-entropy plots concern AMA prompting performance; these are recorded as related findings below, not as tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: AMA is a prompting method paper. It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power laws, and tests no compute allocation, architecture shape or other modality. Its size-related plots show AMA's lift over few-shot and the conditional entropy of RTE predictions under prompting. These are prompting-method effects, not tests of whether downstream performance scales predictably with size or loss (V6). Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only to suggest prompt aggregation as a further scaling axis.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. AMA (QA-format prompt chains plus weak-supervision aggregation) lifts performance across 4 model families from 125M to 175B parameters, by 10.2% absolute on average over few-shot. It lets GPT-J-6B match or beat few-shot GPT3-175B on 15 of 20 benchmarks. The authors draw no conclusion about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies a prompting strategy and does not reproduce or apply the original scaling-law measurement recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: AMA's absolute lift varies with model size and levels out; the reported lift is lower for T0 than for the GPT model families. The paper notes few models per size grouping.

fits_no_version.finding: AMA's absolute lift over few-shot (k=3), averaged over 7 tasks, rises with model size and then levels out. The authors note few models per size group.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The gains from prompt reformatting and aggregation vary with model size and may saturate.

fits_no_version.finding: Conditional entropy H(y|ŷ) on RTE falls as more AMA prompts are aggregated. The authors suggest prompt aggregation may be another scaling axis.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregating more prompts reduces prediction uncertainty, analogous to a scaling axis.

record.problems: The scale-related plots provide no tabulated values; the authors note few models per size grouping. These results do not measure the loss-scaling claims.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss is measured.
All: no fits and no extrapolation.
All: no other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss is not tested. Few-shot accuracy across sizes appears only as a baseline for AMA's lift.
All: no fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: The peer_reviewed field says ICLR 2022. The arXiv v3 is dated Nov 2022, so the venue is likely ICLR 2023; this should be checked. Figure 2 and Figure 7 reuse GPT-3 results from Brown et al. on relative gain from 6.7B to 175B; these are cited results, not the study's own.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether small-run loss fits predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Effects of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling-law forms in other modalities or training regimes.

The study reports downstream task results, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss; its scale-related metric is AMA's lift over a few-shot baseline.
Dependence of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.
